newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania shows few signs of renewal amid collapse.
newsitem.headline: Albania shows few signs of renewal amid collapse.

text.p: Packs of scrawny dogs scavenge through festering mounds of stinking rubbish lining Albania's main north-south road.
The frames of stripped cars litter roadsides and fields in a country where everyone walked 10 years ago and no one could own a car in the rigidly controlled Stalinist state.
Given the decrepit state of the roads, it is no wonder the new national passion, driving, has resulted in a wasteland of thousands of wrecked or abandoned vehicles.
Rusted chassis are used for walls. Bonnets are pounded into roofs, huts or makeshift stands which dot the 260-km (155-mile) road from Shkoder in the north to Vlore in the south.
President Sali Berisha has criss-crossed the country for 10 days, admitting mistakes in handling a recent investment scandal which wiped out the savings of thousands of Albanians.
A trip along the highway shows that while money poured into the pyramid scams during the five years of Berisha's rule, little was invested in developing Europe's poorest country.
Row after row of drab dilapidated concrete apartment blocks stream past, all crumbling. A multitude of satellite dishes jut from drying laundry on balconies in a rare sign of the modern.
There is no hint of maintenance or repair, much less of real development. Everywhere the scenes are of ruin and decay.

Near Shkoder, the main northern Roman Catholic town, an abandoned petrol tanker pokes into the road, quietly rusting since 1995. It is a legacy of Albania's role as a transit point for those busting U.N. sanctions against former Yugoslavia.
Outside the Adriatic port of Durres, west of Tirana, a field is packed with Mercedes, Alfa Romeos, BMWs and Porsches.
Almost every car has a German or Italian national sticker and, according to local taxi drivers, all of them are reputedly stolen and sold with false papers to knowing Albanians.
With no development programme, there is little work. The road is a sea of people: walking, talking, staring. Lambs are slaughtered and skinned along the roadside for Sunday dinner.
A Mercedes screeches to a halt before slamming into one of the many slow-moving donkey carts hauling goods.

Albanians have embraced entrepreneurship. Roadside stands sell honey, soap, tissues, soft drinks, olive oil or just a small bunch of bananas. Those with more money have lined the roads with little one-room bars and cafes.
Berisha's right-wing free-market Democratic Party came to power in 1992. A former communist and heart surgeon, he has pledged to pull the Balkan country into the 20th century.
Yet legacies of Albania's 45 years under the ruthless communist dictator Enver Hoxha abound.
A towering statue of Hoxha as well as statues of Lenin and Stalin were pulled down in Tirana in 1991 after communism fell.
But large fading mosaics and crumbling monuments remain in a style of strong social realism, idealising Albanian workers and peasants, and depicting common struggle and unity.
In Lushnje, south of Tirana, there is a giant stone statue of three peasants, with a woman holding aloft a chaff of wheat. Further north a stone worker raises a hammer.
Perhaps Hoxha's most lasting legacy will be thousands of ugly concrete domes, with slits for machine-guns, cropping out of every hillside, field and village like wild mushrooms.
The pillbox defences were part of Hoxha's plan to protect Albania against imagined enemies, reflecting his own paranoia.
Hoxha banned religion in 1967 and the mixed population of Moslems, Catholics and Orthodox Christians saw their places of worship locked, turned into public buildings or razed.

One rare sign of renewal is the rebuilding of mosques and churches. New minarets and belltowers are silhouetted against snow-capped peaks which run parallel to the north-south road -- part of a forebidding mountain range that has kept Albania separated from its Balkan neighbours for centuries.
